2. Summary

Rivet is a decentralized developer platform that backs up, timestamps, and restores GitHub history using CKB, IPFS, and Arweave. V1 is live on testnet with CCC wallet onboarding, a functional backup engine, 1 click restore, and public developer profiles. The testnet currently runs on free tier hosting.

This proposal requests a grant of $5,000 for Phase 1 of development, covering CoTA frictionless onboarding, the Sovereign Passport (RGB++ Spore DOB), and the production release of the Rivet CLI restore tooling. A follow up proposal will be submitted later for Phase 2, which covers CKB Mainnet deployment, migration to a dedicated domain and VPS hosting, production infrastructure, and audit preparation.

Grant Amount Requested (Phase 1): $5,000
ETA to Completion of Phase 1: 8 weeks from grant approval
CKB Wallet or Funding Address: ckb1qyqvx63t4e0zjk56lldkre9w0225dmuthneq7texcs
Live Demo: https://rivet-web-ten.vercel.app

3. Project Introduction

What problem are you solving?

Developers build their careers, reputations, and open source contributions on platforms they do not control. GitHub can suspend an account overnight with no real appeal process, erasing years of work. If a developer loses access to their account for any reason (suspension, hack, forgotten password, or loss of an old email), they also lose their contribution graph and their proof of authorship. Git commit timestamps are trivially easy to forge, and there is no native cryptographic proof that a specific developer wrote a specific piece of code at a specific time.

What ecosystem or user need does this address?

There are millions of developers worldwide who depend on GitHub as the primary record of their professional work. Every one of them is exposed to the risk of losing that record without warning. Rivet gives developers a decentralized insurance policy. It mirrors their entire repository history to IPFS and Arweave, anchors a cryptographic proof of that history to a CKB Cell, and issues a Sovereign Passport (RGB++ Spore DOB) that proves their developer identity on chain. If anything happens to their account, they can restore everything to a new account with the original history intact.

Why now?

Centralized platforms are becoming less reliable and more censorious. At the same time, CKB’s tooling has matured to the point where this product can be built properly. CCC provides seamless wallet authentication, RGB++ enables Bitcoin bound asset ownership, CoTA enables account abstraction for frictionless onboarding, and Spore DOBs allow for flexible on chain identity. This is the right moment to give developers a real, practical, decentralized alternative for preserving their work.

4. Team and Roles

Name / Handle: Jedi Dtechmaker (jedi_dtechmaker)

Role: Lead Developer, Product Designer, and Project Manager

Experience / Relevant Background:

I am a full stack and Web3 developer with hands on experience across TypeScript, Solidity, JavaScript, Node.js, Go, Rust, Python, and PHP. I have worked extensively with the CKB ecosystem, including CCC for wallet integration and transaction signing, RGB++ for Bitcoin bound assets, and Fiber Network for Layer 2 payments. I am building Rivet because I have personally experienced the frustration of platform dependence and want to give developers a permanent, cryptographically verifiable home for their work.

Links:
GitHub: jedi-dtechmaker (Jedi Dtechmaker) · GitHub
Twitter/X: @jedi_dtechmaker

5. Current Status

Research completed:
Studied existing backup tools (Octarchive, GitPreserver, Vector migrate) and identified their limitations. Researched CKB Cell capacity costs, RGB++ Spore DOB mechanics, CoTA account abstraction, and CCC integration patterns. Defined the two mode restore architecture (Exact Restore versus Attribution Restore) after community feedback.

Prototype and MVP status:

V1 is live on testnet and functional. The web platform is deployed on Vercel and uses GitHub Actions as the backup worker. The CKB anchoring logic is running on testnet with a public verifier page.

What is live and working in V1 (testnet):
GitHub OAuth sign in with one click repo import.
Wallet connect via CCC (JoyID, MetaMask, UniSat). Optional, not required for backups.
Full mirror backup: every branch, tag and commit, dispatched to a GitHub Actions worker.
Merkle root computed over the entire commit history and anchored in a CKB testnet cell, verifiable on chain.
Git bundle pinned to IPFS via Pinata.
Proof panel on every repo with a direct CKB Explorer link.
1 Click Restore on the web: rehydrate a repo with full commit attribution intact.
Auto sync: every git push triggers a fresh backup via GitHub webhook.
Public verify page to look up any proof by CKB tx hash, IPFS CID, or GitHub repo ID.
Public developer profiles, file tree browser, commit history, and README badge generator.
Fully responsive UI with dark mode.

Privacy note for testnet:
Because Rivet is currently serverless, backups run through a public GitHub Actions queue. Private repo names and their IPFS CIDs appear in public logs. AES 256 encryption for private repos is in development. For now, users are advised to back up only public repositories. This is a temporary testnet constraint and will not exist on Mainnet.

Hosting note for testnet:
The platform is currently deployed on Vercel free tier and depends on GitHub Actions for the backup worker. Phase 2 will migrate Rivet to its own dedicated domain and a production VPS, removing the public GitHub Actions dependency entirely and enabling private repository support.

What Phase 1 of this grant will fund:
CoTA frictionless onboarding, the Sovereign Passport, and the production release of the Rivet CLI. A separate Phase 2 proposal will cover CKB Mainnet deployment, dedicated domain and VPS hosting, and production infrastructure.

Community discussion:
I posted the project on CKBuilders Review group and Talknervos and received detailed technical feedback. The key points raised were: separating Exact Restore from Attribution Restore, rewording the timestamp claim to prove repository state existed by a certain block height rather than proving git timestamps themselves, and using CoTA for frictionless onboarding so users never buy CKB. All of these have been incorporated into the design.

6. Application Design

6.1 Functional Overview

Rivet has two interfaces that share the same core engine: a web dashboard for easy onboarding and profile management, and a CLI for developers who want to automate, script, or run restores directly from their terminal.

Web dashboard flow:
A developer signs in with GitHub OAuth. No wallet is required to start. On first backup, a JoyID burner wallet is created silently in the background using WebAuthn and passkeys. Rivet subsidizes the approximately 150 CKB needed to create the user CoTA cell. The developer’s identity and backup proof are stored in a single CoTA Sparse Merkle Tree, compressed into one 32 byte hash on chain.

Rivet then clones the repositories using git clone --mirror, generates a Merkle Tree from the commit hashes, pins the bundle to IPFS via Pinata, and anchors the Merkle root to a CKB Cell. The developer receives a Sovereign Passport (RGB++ Spore DOB) that represents their on chain developer identity.

CLI flow:
The Rivet CLI is a cross platform binary for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Developers can run it locally or inside a CI/CD pipeline.

  • rivet backup <repo> triggers a mirror backup and prints the CKB tx hash and IPFS CID.
  • rivet status <repo> shows the latest anchored proof and block height.
  • rivet verify <tx_hash> independently verifies a proof against CKB and IPFS.
  • rivet restore <repo> --mode exact or --mode attribution performs a full local restore, using git-filter-repo for attribution mode and anchoring a signed hash mapping proof on CKB.
  • rivet watch <dir> monitors a local repository and triggers a backup on every push.

If the developer ever loses access to their GitHub account, they run the Rivet CLI restore command. They choose between Exact Restore (which preserves original commit hashes and the Merkle proof) or Attribution Restore (which remaps old emails to a new email so the contribution graph lights up). Their repositories are pushed to the new account with full history intact, entirely from the terminal.

On chain: CKB Cell storing Merkle roots, RGB++ Spore DOB for identity, CoTA Sparse Merkle Tree for compressed identity storage.
Off chain: Git bundles, IPFS and Arweave storage, PostgreSQL metadata, Next.js frontend, GitHub Actions worker, Rivet CLI.

6.2 Architecture and Design

Smart Contracts and Scripts:
CKB Timestamp Cell script for anchoring Merkle roots.
RGB++ Spore DOB script for the Sovereign Passport.
CoTA Sparse Merkle Tree for compressed identity storage.

Key CKB Features Used:
CCC (@ckb-ccc/core and @ckb-ccc/connector-react) for wallet auth and transaction signing.
CKB Cell model for immutable, decentralized storage of Merkle proofs.
RGB++ for Bitcoin bound asset ownership of the Sovereign Passport.
CoTA for account abstraction and frictionless onboarding.
Spore Protocol for flexible on chain developer identity.

External Dependencies:
IPFS (Pinata) for hot storage.
Arweave for permanent cold storage.
GitHub Actions for backup worker (testnet only, to be replaced in Phase 2).
GitHub OAuth for repository access.

CLI Stack:
Rust or Node.js single binary distribution. git2 or isomorphic-git for local git operations. @ckb-ccc/core for CKB transaction signing.

All core scripts will be open sourced. The full codebase will be publicly available on GitHub.

6.3 Design Rationale

Trade offs considered:
Storing every commit hash on chain would be prohibitively expensive. I use Merkle trees to anchor a single root that represents thousands of commits. This keeps CKB capacity costs low while preserving cryptographic verifiability. For restore, I separate Exact Restore from Attribution Restore because rewriting Git history changes commit hashes, which would break the link to the anchored Merkle root. Exact Restore preserves cryptographic integrity. Attribution Restore offers a signed mapping proof anchored on CKB so the proof chain remains verifiable even after email remapping. For onboarding, I use CoTA because it compresses an entire user dataset into a single 32 byte hash on chain, which makes it viable to subsidize user onboarding and give Web2 developers a seamless experience. The CLI exists because developers need a local, scriptable tool, not just a web UI.

Security considerations:
The Merkle root anchored on CKB proves that a specific repository state existed by a certain CKB block height. It does not prove that the internal git commit timestamps are truthful. I am transparent about this distinction in all UI messaging, CLI output, and documentation.

Alignment with CKB philosophy:
CKB is designed for decentralized state verification and true ownership. Rivet uses CKB exactly as intended: as a permanent, uncensorable notary for developer owned data.

6.4 Fee Model and Sustainability

Rivet will be free for individual developers for basic backup and restore. A premium tier will offer larger storage quotas, private repository backups, priority IPFS pinning, and team features. A small fee will be charged for Arweave permanent storage. Sovereign Passport minting will carry a nominal CKB fee.

Additional revenue streams include B2B API access for credential verification by recruiters and HR platforms, protocol level fees on on chain bounty payments using a Sovereign Passport as escrow, and cryptoeconomic storage staking where node operators stake CKB to guarantee long term repository pinning.

As the user base grows, the platform can sustain itself through these premium features without compromising the free core.

7. Key Benefits for CKB

Network growth: Every backup anchors a transaction on CKB, driving real on chain activity from developers who would not otherwise interact with the network.
Addressing a need: Provides a concrete, practical use case for CKB that solves a real problem for developers worldwide.
Developer tooling: Demonstrates the power of CCC, RGB++, CoTA, and Spore in a production grade application, and ships a cross platform CLI that any developer can install and use immediately.
Community engagement: Onboards Web2 developers into the CKB ecosystem through a tool they actually need.
Interoperability: Uses RGB++ to bind developer identity to Bitcoin, showcasing CKB’s unique position as a Bitcoin Layer 2.

8. Detailed Deliverables and Milestones (Phase 1)

This proposal funds Phase 1 only. Phase 2 will be proposed separately.

Milestone Deliverable(s) Timeline Budget
Milestone 1: CoTA Onboarding and Sovereign Passport CoTA account abstraction integration, JoyID burner wallet creation flow, Rivet subsidized CoTA cell creation, RGB++ Spore DOB minting, public profile integration. Acceptance: end to end onboarding and passport minting live on testnet. Weeks 1 to 4 $2,500
Milestone 2: CLI Restore Tooling and Hardening Cross platform CLI for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Exact and Attribution restore modes, git-filter-repo integration, rivet backup, rivet status, rivet verify, and rivet restore commands. Robust RPC error handling, Auto Sync reliability. Acceptance: CLI published and restore flow verifiable on testnet. Weeks 5 to 8 $2,500

Total Budget for Phase 1: $5,000

9. Budget Breakdown (Phase 1)

Deliverable Budget
Milestone 1: CoTA Onboarding and Sovereign Passport $2,500
Milestone 2: CLI Restore Tooling and Hardening $2,500
Total $5,000

What each milestone covers:

Milestone 1 ($2,500): CoTA Onboarding and Sovereign Passport

  • CoTA account abstraction integration
  • JoyID burner wallet creation flow using WebAuthn and passkeys
  • Rivet subsidized CoTA cell creation (approx. 150 CKB per user)
  • RGB++ Spore DOB minting for the Sovereign Passport
  • Public profile integration to display the passport
  • End to end testing on testnet

Milestone 2 ($2,500): CLI Restore Tooling and Hardening

  • Cross platform CLI binary for Linux, macOS, and Windows
  • Exact and Attribution restore modes
  • git-filter-repo integration for email remapping
  • rivet backup, rivet status, rivet verify, and rivet restore commands
  • Robust RPC error handling and retry logic
  • Auto Sync reliability improvements
  • CLI documentation and usage guide

Infrastructure costs (premium IPFS pinning, production VPS) and audit costs are excluded. They belong to Phase 2.

Payment Schedule:

  • Upfront (50%): $2,500 released upon proposal approval.
  • Upon Completion (50%): $2,500 released after both Phase 1 milestones are delivered and verifiable on testnet.

10. Out of Scope and Future Funding Needs

This proposal covers Phase 1 only. The following items will be addressed in a separate Phase 2 funding request once Phase 1 milestones are delivered:

  • CKB Mainnet deployment: Migrating the anchor layer from testnet to Mainnet.
  • Dedicated domain and VPS hosting: Moving Rivet off Vercel free tier onto its own domain and a production VPS. This removes the dependency on public GitHub Actions for the backup worker and enables private repository support with AES 256 encryption before IPFS upload.
  • Production infrastructure: Premium IPFS pinning, production VPS for cron jobs and the verifier indexer.
  • Security review: Formal third party audit of the CKB scripts and CoTA integration.
  • Long term maintenance: Ongoing IPFS pinning costs and infrastructure scaling.

The Phase 2 proposal will be submitted only after Phase 1 deliverables are complete and verifiable on testnet.

11. Risk and Mitigation

Risk Mitigation
Technical complexity of Merkle proof and restore flow Phased approach with working V1 already live on testnet, open source code, and community feedback at every milestone
Solo developer resource constraints Clear milestones, realistic scope for Phase 1, and active community support
Dependencies on external protocols (IPFS, Arweave) Redundant storage, fallback to local downloads, and monitoring
Community adoption challenges Free tier, CoTA frictionless onboarding so no CKB purchase is required, cross platform CLI for power users, README badge, GitHub Action, and a public demo showing backup, delete, restore, and verify
CoTA subsidy economics Monitor user acquisition cost per onboarded developer. Premium tier revenue must cover subsidy before scaling
Phase 2 funding not approved Phase 1 deliverables are self contained and usable on testnet. If Phase 2 is delayed, the project still functions for testing and community use

12. Closing and Call to Action

Rivet is a practical, developer first tool that brings real utility to CKB. This proposal funds Phase 1, which covers the CoTA onboarding and Sovereign Passport that make the product accessible to non crypto developers, plus the production release of the Rivet CLI that makes the core promise of backup, verify, and restore real for developers who work in the terminal. A Phase 2 proposal will follow for Mainnet deployment, dedicated domain and VPS hosting, and audit preparation. I appreciate your consideration and welcome any feedback or questions from the community.

13. Supporting Links

GitHub Repo: GitHub - jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet · GitHub
Live Demo: https://rivet-web-ten.vercel.app
Architecture Doc: Rivet/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md at main · jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet · GitHub

posts.cooked:
This is a really amazing application of CKB.

Well done, Ma’am

There’s a real problem underneath it, but the blockchain-heavy execution adds more complexity than value.

A few questions before I’d feel good about Phase 1 funding:

  1. Given git is already distributed, the core new value here seems to be the on-chain notarization + one-command restore/reputation portability. Have you looked at how this compares to something like OpenTimestamps, and what CKB specifically buys you over that?
  2. The testnet privacy note is a bit concerning — private repo names and IPFS CIDs leaking into public GitHub Actions logs. Is there a stopgap before Phase 2 (e.g. warning users more prominently, or gating private repo backup entirely) so this doesn’t bite an early adopter?
  3. For the Sovereign Passport/identity angle to matter, someone (recruiters, other devs, platforms) needs to actually check it. Is there a plan for that adoption path?
Thank you boss

Thanks for the questions. Let me answer each quickly and as best as I can.

1. OpenTimestamps vs Rivet

OTS is a timestamping tool. It proves a hash existed at a certain time, but it does not back up your code, restore your repository, or give you an identity. Rivet stores the full Git bundle on IPFS, anchors a Merkle root of the entire commit history on CKB, and provides a one-command restore to a new account with original timestamps and authorship intact. CKB adds a stateful cell model, so the proof can be composed with other scripts, like the RGB++ Spore DOB that acts as your Sovereign Passport. OTS proofs cannot do that.

2. Testnet privacy stopgap

You are right to flag it. Tho like I stated earlier This is temporary,

but here are things I will do during Phase 1, not wait for Phase 2:

· Gate private repo backups entirely on testnet. The option will be disabled with a clear explanation.

· Add a prominent warning on the backup screen if a private repo is selected.

· Update the docs to state the limitation clearly.

Phase 2 fixes it properly with AES 256 encryption and a dedicated VPS worker, removing the public GitHub Actions dependency.

3. Passport adoption path

Start with developers, not recruiters. The CLI and verifier page give developers a shareable proof link and a README badge they can put on their repos. That drives organic exposure. Recruiters and HR platforms come later via the B2B API once there is a critical mass. The first people who will actually check a passport are other CKB developers, and that is fine. It proves the mechanism works in a community that already understands on-chain verification.

I would rather hear pushback now than after Phase 1. The privacy fix happens regardless of funding.

DAO Proposal Sync (Discussion Phase)

This proposal reached 33 likes within the 7-day discussion window and is eligible to proceed to the Metaforo voting stage.

During the window, some community members raised a concern about these likes, so I reviewed them on the final data at the close of the window. No duplicate accounts were found, and all 33 likes stand. Seven of the likes came from accounts created during the window whose only activity has been liking the author’s posts. The full review note follows.

Like Audit: Proposal at [DIS] RIVET: Decentralized GitHub Backup, Timestamping and Restore on CKB

Prepared by: @zz_tovarishch DAO Coordinator
Date: 2026-09-30
Subject: Verification of the 33 likes on the first post of the proposal

1. Background

Some community members raised a concern about the likes on this proposal while its discussion window was still open. As the DAO coordinator, I reviewed the likes using forum administrative data, following the same method as the earlier audit of t/10453. The window closed on 2026-09-29 at 15:53 UTC, and this note uses the final data at that point.

Accounts are identified by their numeric forum user ID. Usernames, email addresses, IP addresses and device details are withheld to avoid exposing personal data and to keep the assessment free of identity bias.

2. Headline finding

The first post had 33 likes when the discussion window closed, and none were added afterward. The review found no evidence that any two of the liking accounts are operated by the same person. It did find 7 accounts that were created after the proposal was published and whose only activity on the forum is liking the author’s posts. Whether these 7 accounts belong to one person or to several people invited by the author cannot be established from forum data.

The remaining 26 likes show no signs of concern. They include long-standing community members.

3. Method and data sources

The review used the same administrative records as t/10453: account creation time, registration IP, last-seen IP, trust level and activity metrics. Two sources were added. The first is the IP address of every recorded login session, which gives a fuller network history than the registration and last-seen snapshots. Because Discourse overwrites a session’s IP address when it refreshes the session, these were collected twice, on 2026-09-28 and again after the window closed, and both sets were compared. The second is each account’s complete like history with timestamps. Discourse’s own similar-user count, which flags accounts sharing an IP address, was also checked. User IDs are issued strictly in registration order.

4. Evidence

4.1 No shared network identity

Across all 33 liking accounts and the author’s account, and across every recorded login session in both collections (117 distinct IP addresses), no IP address is shared by any two accounts. Discourse’s similar-user count links none of them to one another. The author’s IP addresses carry no other forum account. This is the decisive difference from t/10453, where the proposal author’s own account shared an IP address with eight of the liking accounts.

4.2 Seven single-purpose accounts

All seven registered between 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-26, after the proposal was published on 2026-09-22. Each liked the proposal within minutes of registering, and every like any of them has given on the forum went to the author’s posts. None has posted, and total reading time ranges from 7 seconds to about 3 minutes.

User ID Registered (UTC) Registration to like Likes given in total Of which on the author’s posts Total read time Days visited
4472 2026-09-23 12:30 41 min 2 2 ~3 min 1
4478 2026-09-23 20:15 19 s 1 1 7 s 1
4482 2026-09-24 17:00 ~2 min 1 1 13 s 1
4483 2026-09-24 18:19 ~6 min 4 4 ~2 min 3
4485 2026-09-25 17:29 ~6 min 2 2 ~2 min 1
4489 2026-09-26 08:34 51 s 1 1 ~2 min 1
4490 2026-09-26 08:40 ~2 min 1 1 40 s 2

Account 4472’s first like, 29 seconds after it registered, went to the author’s earlier topic on the same project.

4.3 What the evidence does not show

The seven accounts use a different IP address in every session, spread across three mobile carriers and four days. The author also switches between carriers, so this spread fits either one person using several SIM cards or several different people. One of the seven (4478) uses the same uncommon desktop configuration as one of the author’s sessions, but a device type is not an identifier and the IP addresses differ. Some of the seven fall in the same carrier address blocks as the author. On shared mobile networks this indicates at most that they are in the same area.

4.4 Context

The same behavior appears elsewhere in the same registration window. Among accounts created between 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-27, several others registered and then liked a single proposal, and those proposals belong to other authors. Registering in order to support one proposal is therefore not specific to this proposal. This observation is context only and is not a review of those proposals (see Section 7).

5. Assessment against prior practice

The prior practice this DAO relies on comes from Growing the Italian ecosystem (talk.nervos.org/t/growing-the-italian-ecosystem/7707).

Growing the Italian Ecosystem

It’s been 7 days, after removing likes from users who voted multiple times, this proposal didn’t reach 30 likes.

The element that justified removal there was one person liking through several accounts. That element is not established here.

In the audit of t/10453, seven accounts without a direct IP link were also excluded. They were excluded because their user IDs sat inside an unbroken registration run together with accounts already tied to the author by shared IP, so they belonged to an operation whose single operator had been shown. Here no operator has been shown, and the seven accounts are interleaved with unrelated new accounts that liked other proposals. The inference that supported the earlier exclusion is not available.

Excluding these seven likes would therefore mean treating newly created, single-purpose accounts as ineligible to like. That would be a new standard rather than an application of prior practice.

6. Conclusion

The DAO’s metarules contain no provision on who may like a proposal during the discussion phase, the coordinator holds no authority to invalidate support by fiat, and the prior practice does not reach these accounts. The seven likes are therefore not removed. The count for the discussion-phase threshold remains 33, and the proposal is eligible to proceed to the Metaforo voting stage.

Whether likes from accounts created only to support a proposal should count toward the threshold is a question the metarules do not currently answer. If the DAO wants such a rule, for example a minimum account age or level of activity for a like to count, it should be adopted through the normal process and applied to all proposals going forward rather than to this proposal alone.

7. Scope of this review

As with the audit of t/10453, this review was triggered only because a specific concern was raised while the proposal was live. It creates no standing audit, places no obligation on the coordinator to review other proposals, and does not reopen proposals whose discussion windows have already closed.

8. Availability of the evidence

The complete underlying records are held by the coordinator and are independently visible to forum administrators through the forum’s admin tools. Any DAO member may request to review the basis for this note and will receive the pseudonymized evidence record in the same form as this note. Raw personal data such as email addresses, IP addresses and device details is not redistributed. Where a member wants those values confirmed, forum administrators can do so directly.
Please if you are a DAO member please Vote for me https://dao.ckb.community/thread/vot-rivet-decentralized-github-backup-timestamping-and-restore-on-ckb-80044

Nice work getting a working demo on testnet. Backup with a restore path is a real gap, and splitting restore into Exact and Attribution modes is the right call. Two technical points:

1. Anchoring for the deletion case. If GitHub deletes the repo, the anchor is the only independent reference left. What matters then is: does the restored copy match what was backed up? Anchoring a hash of the sorted refs and their tip commits answers that directly. After restore, anyone can recompute it from the bundle with plain git and compare it to the cell, with no GitHub and no Rivet server involved. Most repos are still SHA-1, so I’d also anchor a SHA-256 of the bundle itself. That lets the copy retrieved from IPFS or Arweave be checked byte for byte before restoring.

2. Cell lifecycle and cost per push. With auto-sync on every push, do you consume the previous anchor cell into the new one, or create a fresh cell each time? Consuming and replacing keeps locked capacity flat, and the transaction chain becomes the version history for free. Creating new cells makes the subsidy grow with activity. This is the model I use in VeriCell.net (disclosure: I build it). Each new version consumes the previous live cell, so the live cell always shows the current state and older versions stay verifiable as consumed cells. Happy to compare notes if a shared manifest or verification format makes sense.

Good luck with the vote.

posts.cooked:
Thanks for the feedback and the vote!

To answer your questions.

  1. Anchoring & deletion case: Great point. Right now we Merkle-tree all commit hashes (git log --all), but you’re spot on about refs and tip commits. Adding the sorted refs hash + a SHA-256 of the bundle itself makes offline CLI verification (git show-ref / sha256sum) trivial without touching our servers. We’re adding both to the anchor payload.

  2. Cell lifecycle: We already consume and replace! Each backup takes the previous anchor cell as an input and outputs the updated one. Capacity stays locked flat at ~93 CKB per repo, and the transaction chain gives us the immutable version history for free.

And i am definitely down to compare notes!!!
And i really love the idea and concept behind your product VeriCell.

Based on the Metaforo tally at close, the outcome is PASSED. Approval is 52.82% with total voting weight 244,888,704 CKB.

Post-close verification has been completed using CKB DAO Watchdog (GitHub - CKBFansDAO/ckb-dao-watchdog: Community-driven tools for auditing and verifying CKB DAO governance voting results. · GitHub), together with a manual sanity check. The verification cross-checks Metaforo-recorded voting weights against on-chain Nervos DAO deposit weights. In this run, 21 of 22 entries match.

One Yes entry is flagged in the log because the voter’s current on-chain deposit is 300,000 CKB higher than the weight Metaforo recorded. The difference comes from a single new deposit made after the vote was cast. The deposits held at the time of voting match the recorded weight exactly, and none of them has been withdrawn since. The vote was therefore counted at its vote-time weight, which is lower than the voter’s current deposit. Counting the later deposit would raise approval to 52.87%, so the flag does not change the outcome.

No voter appears under both options, and no address is bound to more than one voting account.

The RIVET proposal is confirmed as PASSED.

  • Hosted application: rivet-web-ten.vercel.app
  • Dashboard: rivet-web-ten.vercel.app/dashboard
  • Funded proposal and discussion: Rivet: Decentralized GitHub Backup, Timestamping and Restore on CKB
  • Milestone checklist: Phase One milestones
  • Latest implementation release in this report: commit ff5b040

Milestone 1 deliverables

The three Milestone 1 deliverables map to the implementation as follows:

Deliverable Delivered behavior Review evidence
CoTA onboarding Rivet-sponsored activation creates a CoTA cell under the developer’s verified JoyID lock; the developer can claim and update identity and backup commitments. Registration, issuer, claim, and update transactions linked below.
Optional JoyID connection GitHub backups work without a wallet; connecting JoyID starts account-bound ownership verification before on-chain activation. Hosted dashboard, wallet-proof implementation, and completed hosted onboarding checks.
Sovereign Passport A verified manifest snapshot is minted as a wallet-owned Spore digital object, with saved mint plans, exact retries, and public-profile integration. Passport mint, Spore ID, implementation, and completed ownership/privacy checks linked below.

GitHub onboarding and sponsored CoTA identity

Rivet connects repository backup evidence to a developer-controlled on-chain identity. GitHub remains the starting point: a developer signs in and can back up public repositories without first creating or connecting a wallet. The backup flow mirrors repository history, produces a Git bundle, pins it to IPFS, and anchors its commit-set commitment on CKB. Developers who want an on-chain identity can then connect JoyID from the dashboard.

Wallet linking requires a server-issued ownership challenge bound to the account, wallet, origin, and expiry. JoyID’s passkey signature is verified before the wallet is linked to the GitHub identity. An address submitted by itself is insufficient. The connected developer then activates a sponsored CoTA identity, with the resulting cell locked to their verified JoyID wallet.

The initial confirmed registration provided 150 test CKB of capacity through Rivet sponsorship. Users do not need to acquire that capacity themselves to activate their identity. Registration and transaction state are persisted so retries can recover the existing operation.

  • Sponsored registration: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Ownership and onboarding implementation: WalletIdentity
  • Server-side passkey and wallet verification: wallet-proof.ts

User-owned CoTA manifests and backup proofs

The CoTA manifest lifecycle now supports issuance, owner-approved claim, and subsequent backup updates. A dedicated Rivet issuer creates the metadata records, and the developer claims them into their JoyID-owned CoTA tree. Later updates add completed public backup proofs with explicit JoyID approval. The records commit the full 32-byte manifest root; the exported manifest provides the identity and backup records needed to reconstruct and check that commitment.

The manifest format is versioned as rivet-cota-manifest-v1. Its binding includes the CKB network, immutable GitHub account ID, owner and issuer lock hashes, collection ID, and two distinct token indexes. Developer records bind the GitHub identity to the wallet lock. Backup records contain the immutable repository ID, repository name, IPFS CID, commit-set Merkle root, anchor outpoint, and commit count. Record keys use immutable repository IDs so a repository name alone cannot substitute a different repository.

Two CoTA metadata records carry the complete root: the first characteristic stores 20 bytes, and the second stores the remaining 12 bytes with canonical padding. Verification reconstructs the full root and checks the manifest records against it. The Git bundle itself remains in IPFS.

Independent manifest verification checks the configured issuer binding, JoyID ownership approval, issuance and claim references, the reconstructed manifest commitment, and the referenced backup anchor through public CKB Testnet RPC. The verified backup snapshot contains one public backup proof and one verified backup anchor.

  • Issuer registration: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Metadata collection definition: CKB Testnet transaction
  • JoyID-approved claim: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Initial independently verified backup update: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Latest confirmed manifest update: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Verification procedure: CoTA manifest runbook
  • Standalone verifier: verify-cota-manifest.ts

Independent verification

The public testnet identifiers used by this release are:

  • Manifest collection ID: 0x8340e0bf4c432def07fef3bae8d46f43569bf4f8.
  • Trusted issuer lock hash: 0xf2834302ab71b9094c16c1507e9ce2289dade32b444491d557da1c439c8f8579.
  • Exported proof format: rivet-cota-manifest-proof-v1.
  • Record encoding and commitment construction: cota-manifest.ts.
  • Chain-based proof checks: cota-manifest-verify.ts.

Reviewers can download the manifest proof from the dashboard, independently compare the issuer lock hash against the public deployment evidence, and run the standalone verifier from the repository root:

pnpm --filter @rivet/web exec tsx scripts/verify-cota-manifest.ts \
  --proof /absolute/path/rivet-cota-manifest-proof.json \
  --issuer-lock-hash 0xf2834302ab71b9094c16c1507e9ce2289dade32b444491d557da1c439c8f8579

The verifier reads transaction references from the proof package and retrieves committed transaction data from the selected public RPC. It reconstructs the issuance, claim, and update lineage and checks each backup root against its referenced anchor output. It requires neither Rivet database credentials nor an issuer private key. A proof cannot select its own trusted issuer.

Backup sync and retry behavior

The dashboard shows one stored public backup, one synced proof, and no newer completed backup awaiting sync. Independent verification of the latest manifest and current passport ownership was included in the completed project acceptance checks.

Existing backups can be reconciled into the manifest without uploading another bundle or producing another backup anchor. Preparation also detects an unchanged confirmed snapshot before reserving another publication operation. Approved transaction bytes are saved for exact retries after an uncertain submission. Live acceptance confirmed that disconnecting, reloading, and reconnecting the same wallet preserves the synchronized state without another transaction or fee when the records are unchanged.

Sovereign Passport

The Sovereign Passport is implemented as a Spore V2 digital object owned through the developer’s verified JoyID wallet. Its immutable JSON content records the GitHub identity, initial owner lock hash, manifest root, and manifest transaction reference. The passport preserves the verified snapshot selected at mint time; a later backup update can advance the current manifest independently.

Passport content uses rivet-sovereign-passport-v1 with the content type application/json. Mint validation checks the Spore type, identifier, owner lock, and exact saved content. Approval may replace the JoyID lock signature but cannot alter the prepared outputs, fees, dependencies, or other saved witnesses. Public-profile verification checks both the confirmed mint and the live Spore cell, so transferred or no-longer-live passports can be distinguished from passports still held by the linked wallet.

The confirmed real-wallet mint is recorded here:

  • Passport mint: CKB Testnet transaction
  • Spore ID: 0x3354b38df9a9a245cc01aabf57be83529bc97d826844fb72f156ce02458d0aad
  • Locked capacity: 759 test CKB.
  • Network fee: 0.00013595 test CKB.
  • Mint implementation: passport-service.ts
  • Passport content and approval validation: passport.ts
  • Public manifest and current ownership verification: public-identity.ts

The wallet funds the passport from ordinary capacity cells and approves the transaction through JoyID. The CoTA identity cell and other typed assets are excluded from funding selection. For the test demonstration, the wallet received an authorized treasury top-up before minting. The capacity locked in the passport is separate from the transaction fee.

Mint preparation reserves one saved plan per GitHub identity. Submission validates the approved transaction, persists the first valid signed candidate, and reuses that exact transaction during retries. Live refresh and retry checks returned the same mint without a duplicate mint or additional fee.

Dashboard and public-profile presentation

Public profiles now have a developer-passport panel that verifies exported manifest references and checks whether the live Spore remains owned by the linked wallet. Private profiles suppress public identity proofs. The dashboard and profile also present a visual passport card, green activation and sync indicators, compact backup statistics, expandable transaction details, and refresh controls with loading, success, and failure feedback.

The current passport’s on-chain content is JSON. The graphic card is an application presentation of that object; its artwork is not embedded in the minted Spore. The implementation does not include a Bitcoin RGB++ binding or a DOB image-renderer protocol.

Delivery decisions and general availability

Several implementation choices clarify the proposal’s delivery model. Wallet onboarding starts when a developer chooses Connect Wallet, rather than being required for the first backup. The CoTA manifest uses the supported metadata lifecycle after an earlier custom extension proved incompatible with the deployed JoyID lock. Historical signed-witness proofs remain available, but they are not counted as satisfying the CoTA SMT storage requirement.

Registration is designed for general use. There is no hardcoded user allowlist, and manifest enrollment has no account cap by default. Identity sponsorship has a separate configurable capacity budget. The shared issuer and collection are Rivet infrastructure used to issue records for eligible users; each developer’s identity cell and passport are associated with their own verified wallet.

Testing and validation

Automated validation for implementation commit ff5b040 recorded:

  • 139 web checks passed, with zero failures and 13 environment-dependent checks skipped.
  • TypeScript checking passed.
  • The CLI test file passed.
  • Git whitespace checks passed.

Earlier engineering sessions recorded additional disposable-PostgreSQL and deployed-script validation, including wallet-proof rejection, proof tampering, concurrent approval handling, additive schema upgrades, and saved transaction retries. Those results are documented in the repository’s acceptance material. They were not all rerun in the latest pre-push check, and no external security audit is claimed.

The published tests make the main failure cases reviewable:

  • Wallet ownership tests reject mismatched challenges, malformed proofs, credentials belonging to another wallet, and unsupported wallet types.
  • Manifest verification tests reject substituted issuers or GitHub identities, unconfirmed transactions, incorrect RPC transaction hashes, missing approval witnesses, inconsistent roots, incorrect backup anchors, and updates disconnected from the declared claim.
  • Passport tests cover content and owner validation, immutable approval boundaries, saved-mint retries, and ordinary-wallet-cell funding selection.
  • Passport database tests cover concurrent signature acceptance and repeat additive migrations preserving saved mint bytes. These require disposable PostgreSQL and belong to the environment-dependent integration checks.

Validation references

  • Test sources: web tests
  • Release-check workflow: checks.yml
  • Acceptance procedure: Passport and onboarding acceptance

Completed hosted acceptance

Hosted configuration and proof availability have been resolved and checked. The completed Milestone 1 acceptance covers:

  • The hosted flow from GitHub sign-in and wallet-free backup through wallet verification, sponsored activation, claim, backup sync, passport mint, and public-profile display.
  • Disconnect, reload, and reconnect to the same wallet, followed by unchanged sync without another transaction or fee.
  • Passport refresh and retry returning the same mint without a duplicate transaction or fee.
  • Independent verification of the latest manifest and current passport ownership, plus public/private profile checks.
  • Consolidation and checking of explorer references and screenshots or video for reviewer inspection.

Next milestone

The next milestone covers CLI restore tooling and hardening. Initial source commands for backup, status, legacy-proof verification, and exact restore are present, with local recovery checks after removing the original repository. Published cross-platform releases, attribution restore with signed mapping proofs, stronger anchor payloads binding refs and bundle bytes, and live restore acceptance remain ahead.

Verification scope

Rivet remains on CKB Testnet, with private repository backups disabled in this flow. Its anchors establish repository-state commitments at blockchain checkpoints; they do not certify developer-supplied Git commit dates or guarantee current IPFS availability.

The trust boundaries are explicit: Rivet’s issuer attests the GitHub identity association, the selected CKB RPC supplies committed status and chain data, and the verifier checks the referenced snapshot and its commitments. It is not an independent block-header verifier, and snapshot verification does not establish that no newer CoTA update exists. Current file availability is separate from proof validity.

Community review

Milestone 1 is ready for community review. Useful independent checks include:

  • Sign in with GitHub, back up a public repository without connecting a wallet, and inspect the resulting CKB anchor and IPFS reference.
  • Connect a CKB Testnet JoyID wallet, verify ownership, and follow the sponsored identity, manifest claim, and backup-sync flow.
  • Download the manifest proof and run the standalone verification command above.
  • Review the displayed passport capacity and fee before minting; reconnect and refresh to confirm the same saved mint is returned.
  • Inspect the public profile and its transaction links, then check that private-profile visibility suppresses public identity proofs.

Please share test results, unexpected behavior, or integration questions in the proposal thread or through GitHub Issues.

Rivet Milestone 2: CLI Restore Tooling and Hardening

Delivery update · November 21, 2026 · CKB Testnet

Implementation and project acceptance testing for Rivet’s second grant milestone are complete.

Milestone 2 delivers a published cross-platform CLI, independent Exact Restore, Attribution Restore with signed commit mappings, separate mapping commitments on CKB Testnet, stronger backup commitments, and improvements to transaction recovery, backup-job coordination, and Auto Sync reliability.

The current published preview is cli-v0.1.0-rc.4. It includes the unchanged-backup waiting fix and works with the deployed server’s duplicate-snapshot protection. The custom-domain configuration is also complete: GitHub sign-in through tryrivet.xyz has been checked in a real browser and successfully reaches the dashboard.

Together with Milestone 1’s GitHub-first onboarding, verified wallet linking, user-owned CoTA identity, manifest lifecycle, and Sovereign Passport, this completes the implementation and recorded project acceptance work for the funded Phase One Testnet scope.

I’m sharing the delivery evidence and would appreciate feedback from developers who try the tools, inspect the proofs, or have ideas for integration.

  • Repository: jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet
  • Official website: tryrivet.xyz
  • Dashboard: www.tryrivet.xyz/dashboard
  • Published CLI: cli-v0.1.0-rc.4
  • Release source: commit a17f810
  • Funded proposal and discussion: Rivet: Decentralized GitHub Backup, Timestamping and Restore on CKB
  • Recorded live acceptance: Milestone 2 acceptance procedure and results
  • Public evidence: Proofs, recovery comparisons, signed mapping, transaction checks, and release records

CLI and recovery

Rivet now provides an installable npm archive and standalone executables for Linux x64, macOS arm64, and Windows x64, with SHA-256 checksum files. The npm installation requires Node.js 24 or later; the standalone executables include their runtime. Git is required for repository recovery.

Install the current preview:

npm install --global https://github.com/jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet/releases/download/cli-v0.1.0-rc.4/rivet-cli-0.1.0.tgz

rivet --version
rivet --help

Developers first sign in to the web dashboard with GitHub, then authenticate the CLI for the same account:

rivet login --server https://www.tryrivet.xyz

CLI login uses a hidden GitHub personal-access-token prompt. Saved credentials are bound to the selected server origin, and the personal token is not forwarded to the backup worker.

From a repository directory, Rivet can detect the GitHub repository from its origin remote. An explicit repository argument also works:

rivet backup owner/repository

rivet status owner/repository \
  --proof-out /private/location/project-recovery.secret.json

The hosted worker mirrors pushed GitHub history, creates and encrypts a Git bundle, uploads it to IPFS, and anchors the repository-state commitment on CKB Testnet. Public-repository backup does not require a connected wallet.

The recovery export contains the decryption material needed for independent recovery. It belongs in private storage outside version control.

With that recovery file retained, verification and Exact Restore can run after logout:

rivet logout

rivet verify \
  --proof /private/location/project-recovery.secret.json

rivet restore --mode exact \
  --proof /private/location/project-recovery.secret.json \
  --target ./recovered.git

git -C ./recovered.git fsck --full --strict

git clone ./recovered.git ./working-copy

Exact Restore creates a new bare Git mirror while preserving original commit IDs, branches, and tag objects. It does not require the original GitHub repository or a saved Rivet login. The verifier checks the referenced CKB commitment and recovered bundle before accepting the result.

Attribution Restore creates a separate rewritten mirror using an explicit email mapping and git-filter-repo 2.47.0. Its output retains:

  • original.git: the exact verified original mirror.
  • rewritten.git: the mirror containing the selected attribution changes.
  • mapping.json: an Ed25519-signed document linking the original and rewritten commits and committing the rewritten refs.

Independent mapping verification reproduces the rewrite and checks every commit mapping, the rewritten refs, and the signature against the selected trusted public key.

Rewriting changes commit IDs and removes original commit and tag signatures from the rewritten copy. The exact original mirror preserves those objects. Email remapping does not independently establish original authorship or guarantee GitHub contribution-graph eligibility.

The signed mapping can also be committed through a separate CKB Testnet transaction. Its submission flow saves the signed transaction before broadcast and reuses the same transaction during recovery from an interrupted submission.

Implementation and reproduction instructions are available in the CLI guide and attribution proof specification.

Recorded Testnet acceptance

The live acceptance repository was jedi-dtechmaker/DEXsol-skannar. Its selected snapshot contained three commits, two branches, and one annotated tag.

Two v2 backup transactions demonstrated the backup-anchor replacement lifecycle. A separate transaction then committed the signed attribution mapping.

Operation Confirmed transaction Block height Locked capacity Network fee
First v2 backup 8bb202bc… 23131379 225 test CKB 0.00000672 test CKB
Successor v2 backup 707f7244… 23131463 225 test CKB 0.00000672 test CKB
Separate mapping anchor 09e362fc… 23131676 97 test CKB 0.000005 test CKB

The two backup rows represent successive versions of one backup anchor. The successor consumes the preceding backup cell; they are not two simultaneously live 225-CKB backup cells.

Exact and attribution recovery used the first v2 snapshot. The mapping transaction used ordinary treasury change from the second backup transaction and left its backup-anchor output untouched. Locked capacity is separate from the network fee.

The recorded recovery checks established that:

  • All three original commit IDs and all three refs matched after Exact Restore.
  • The annotated tag object was preserved.
  • git fsck --full --strict passed.
  • Attribution verification independently reproduced every commit mapping and rewritten ref.
  • The published npm CLI and Linux executable verified the signed mapping and its separate Testnet anchor.

The original live-chain acceptance used the published rc.3 CLI. The current rc.4 release adds the subsequent unchanged-backup compatibility fix, with the release and regression validation described below.

The exact-recovery run used an empty credential directory, an unavailable Rivet origin, and a source mirror removed from its original path. CLI fetch calls were restricted to the selected CKB RPC and public IPFS gateways, while Git transport was restricted to local files.

The supporting evidence includes:

  • Exact recovery and complete commit/ref comparison
  • Signed attribution mapping
  • Owner public key
  • Mapping funding, lifecycle, capacity, and fee checks
  • Published CLI mapping verification

The mapping’s public identifiers are:

  • Signed-document digest: 0xb48332694b9924e211e1e309ab5eb0662b0d755e0d25a7f90ee5829827e7d792
  • Owner public-key fingerprint: 0x4bd3634d95988d3e07061a4be22097a7e4dae5f238e0791c974fedc02dbd83a8
  • Mapping output index: 0

The owner key is distributed through the repository’s established publication channel. A key embedded in a mapping document alone does not establish its owner’s identity.

Backup protection and hardening

The v2 backup commitment binds the commit-set root, sorted refs and their object IDs, plaintext Git-bundle SHA-256, encrypted IPFS CID, and commit count.

This strengthens verification beyond the older root-only anchors. Legacy proofs retain their original verification limits; exporting an older proof does not upgrade its on-chain commitment.

The duplicate-snapshot fix is deployed. When repository identity, history, and refs match a confirmed, live v2 backup, the worker checks the retained recovery material and reuses that backup. A matching result avoids another bundle upload or backup-anchor transaction. Changed branches or tags still require a new snapshot, including changes that leave the commit count unchanged.

The two backup transactions in the historical acceptance table predate this optimization and demonstrate successor-cell replacement.

The published rc.4 CLI follows the specific backup job and accepts a confirmed unchanged result using the existing transaction hash. This resolves the earlier waiting behavior that expected a different transaction hash even when the server had correctly reused the existing backup.

Additional hardening includes:

  • One active backup reservation per repository, duplicate-delivery detection, and coalesced follow-up work.
  • Saved signed transaction checkpoints and reconciliation using the saved transaction hash.
  • Reuse of the same signed transaction bytes during submission recovery.
  • Current-head checks and replay-safe completion callbacks that preserve newer repository state.
  • Bounded retries for transient RPC reads.
  • Webhook reactivation, secret refresh, pagination, and bounded setup concurrency.

Configured worker quotas continue to apply.

The implementation records include security and hardening PR #3 and the unchanged-backup follow-up in PR #4.

Release and validation

The rc.4 release is published from commit a17f81017d41b38db8baff7e1497c1a4d257ba18.

Both public workflows completed successfully:

  • CLI release workflow: Linux, macOS, and Windows build and installed-command checks, followed by publication.
  • Release checks: web checks and CLI checks across Linux, macOS, and Windows.

The public rc.4 npm archive was independently downloaded, hashed, installed outside the Rivet checkout, and exercised against the unchanged-backup regression. The installed command completed successfully with the existing transaction hash and exported the matching recovery proof.

The published checksum files matched GitHub’s application-asset digests. Native execution is covered by the successful platform release matrix.

Recorded source-update validation included:

  • 211 web checks passed, with zero failures and five optional deployed-script checks skipped.
  • 20 CLI checks passed, with zero failures.
  • Disposable-PostgreSQL concurrency and callback-replay checks passed.
  • TypeScript checking, the production build, and Git whitespace checks passed.
  • Worker fixtures checked that unchanged history skips bundling, encryption, upload, and broadcast, including resumed jobs.

The recorded negative checks rejected a wrong recovery key, altered refs commitment, modified encrypted bundle, tampered mapping signature, and an existing restore destination.

Release CI also includes dependency auditing. These results describe project acceptance, regression testing, and dependency checks; they do not constitute an independent third-party security audit.

Official domain

Rivet is now available at tryrivet.xyz, with www.tryrivet.xyz as the canonical application address.

The custom-domain GitHub callback and login-cookie host are aligned. The final browser check confirmed successful GitHub sign-in and dashboard access.

The previous Vercel website address remains an entry point and redirects browser pages to the official domain. Its API routes remain directly available for existing CLI clients.

Seven live routing/API checks and the OAuth initiation check passed. The hosted application continues to use CKB Testnet.

Scope and verification boundaries

Current hosted backups cover public repository history pushed to GitHub. Unpushed commits, uncommitted files, arbitrary local folders, and private repositories are outside this Testnet flow.

Independent recovery requires the exported recovery material and an available encrypted bundle, retrieved from IPFS or retained locally. The public evidence excludes recovery keys, GitHub tokens, CKB private keys, and the mapping-signing private key.

An anchor establishes a repository-state commitment by a CKB block height. It does not certify developer-supplied commit dates or original authorship. The CLI relies on the selected RPC for committed status and block-header data; it is not an independent consensus verifier.

IPFS availability remains separate from proof validity. During acceptance, recovery succeeded through an alternative public gateway and from a saved encrypted bundle.

Vellum integration direction

We are also exploring an optional integration with Vellum.

The first integration being considered is verified did:ckb linking and displaying relevant, trusted Vellum claims alongside Rivet’s Sovereign Passport. A later extension could provide portable Rivet backup receipts referencing confirmed repository snapshots.

This is proposed follow-on work for discussion with Vellum’s maintainer and the community. It is outside the completed Milestone 2 deliverables. The intended scope keeps identity and evidence sharing optional while preserving Rivet’s independent backup and recovery flow.

Feedback on useful claim formats, ownership verification, issuer trust, and applications that could consume Rivet evidence would be welcome.

Phase One completion and next phase

The implementation and recorded project acceptance work for both funded Phase One milestones are complete:

  • Milestone 1: GitHub-first onboarding, verified wallet linking, sponsored user-owned CoTA identity, manifest commitments, Sovereign Passport, and profile verification.
  • Milestone 2: Published cross-platform CLI, independent exact and attribution recovery, signed and anchored mappings, stronger backup commitments, and backup/RPC reliability improvements.

For anyone who wants to explore the delivery, useful checks include:

  1. Install rc.4 for your operating system and verify its checksum.
  2. Back up an authorized public repository and retain its private recovery export.
  3. Repeat an unchanged backup and check that the existing confirmed transaction is reused.
  4. Log out, restore into a new destination, compare commits and refs, and run Git integrity checks.
  5. Try Attribution Restore and verify its complete signed mapping using an independently established owner key.
  6. Inspect the linked Testnet transactions and compare their commitments with the published evidence.

The next proposed phase focuses on dedicated worker hosting, monitoring and recovery procedures, authorized encrypted private-repository backups, durable storage and retention, independent security review and remediation, CKB Mainnet rollout, and operating budgets. Scope, funding, schedule, and acceptance criteria will be agreed separately. The official domain and its GitHub sign-in configuration are already completed.

I would appreciate reviews, test results, integration ideas, and suggestions from the community. If you try Rivet or inspect the delivery evidence, please share your experience in this proposal thread or through GitHub Issues.

Thank you to everyone following Rivet’s progress and taking the time to try the tools or share feedback.
